# Reproducible Data Science {#sec-quarto}

Quarto turns plain-text source into reproducible documents that combine
explanation, computation, results, figures, and references. A data-science
analysis should be reproducible because readers need to inspect how evidence
was produced, not merely see a final picture or a pasted table. Quarto supports
Python, R, Julia, and Observable and can publish articles, reports, websites,
books, and presentations in several output formats [@quarto2025guide].

This chapter is a jump start, not a replacement for the [complete Quarto
Guide](https://quarto.org/docs/guide/). Use the guide when you need options not
covered here, and consult the [Python documentation](https://quarto.org/docs/computations/python.html),
[Markdown reference](https://quarto.org/docs/authoring/markdown-basics.html),
and [presentation documentation](https://quarto.org/docs/presentations/)
for detailed examples [@quarto2025python; @quarto2025markdown;
@quarto2025presentations].

## A Minimal Quarto Document

A Quarto document is a text file whose `.qmd` extension combines YAML
metadata, Markdown prose, equations, citations, and executable code chunks.
The following small document is a better starting point than a code-only
hello-world: it produces a numerical result, a table, and a figure from the
same code that explains them.

Create a file named `hello.qmd` with YAML metadata like this:

```yaml
---
title: "Hello, Quarto"
author: "Your Name"
format: html
jupyter: python3
bibliography: references.bib
---
```

The document can then combine prose, equations, and executable code. Equation
punctuation follows ordinary sentence punctuation. The mean of observations
$x_1,\ldots,x_n$ is given by @eq-mean.

The source syntax for this numbered equation is:

```text
The mean ... is given by @eq-mean.

$$
\bar{x} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i.
$$ {#eq-mean}
```

$$
\bar{x} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i.
$$ {#eq-mean}

A cases display can continue a sentence with a comma, as shown in @eq-cases:

$$
g(x) =
\begin{cases}
  0, & x < 0,\\
  1, & x \ge 0.
\end{cases}
$$ {#eq-cases}

The comma after the first case and the period after the final case are part of
one grammatical statement. The code below generates a table and a figure from
the same observations:

```{python}
#| label: fig-scores
#| fig-cap: "Scores for three students"
#| fig-format: svg
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import pandas as pd
from matplotlib_inline.backend_inline import set_matplotlib_formats

set_matplotlib_formats("svg")

scores = pd.DataFrame({"student": ["A", "B", "C"],
                       "score": [82, 91, 87]})
scores["score"].mean()
scores

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.bar(scores["student"], scores["score"])
ax.set(xlabel="Student", ylabel="Score", title="Scores")
plt.show()
```

The resulting table and Figure @fig-scores summarize the observations above.
Quarto itself is documented in the Quarto Guide [@quarto2025guide].

The opening and closing lines between `---` define YAML metadata. Headings use
one or more `#` characters, ordinary text forms paragraphs, dollar signs mark
LaTeX equations, and a fenced code chunk begins with ```` ```{python} ````. The
`jupyter: python3` setting tells Quarto which Jupyter kernel should execute
Python chunks. Expressions whose values are displayed, such as `scores`, and
figures returned by the chunk become part of the rendered document.

Render the document from its directory:

```bash
quarto render hello.qmd
```

Quarto writes `hello.html` by default. Open that file in a browser, or use
`quarto preview hello.qmd` while editing to render again after each save. Keep
the `.qmd` source under version control; treat the rendered HTML as generated
output.

## Markdown Essentials

Markdown provides the readable structure around an analysis. The following
constructs cover the structures needed in early assignments:

````markdown
# Chapter title
## Section heading

**bold**, *italic*, and [a link](https://quarto.org/)

- an unordered list
- another item

1. a numbered step
2. another step

`inline code` and a code block:

```python
print("This block is displayed, not executed by Quarto.")
```

> A block quote highlights a definition or key point.

| quantity | value |
|:--|--:|
| observations | 3 |
| mean | 86.7 |

![A descriptive caption](figures/scores.png)

See the Quarto Guide [@quarto2025guide] and @eq-mean.
````

Use a heading hierarchy rather than bold text to organize a document. Put a
blank line around paragraphs and lists, write descriptive link text, and keep
code that should execute in a Quarto code chunk. Use a meaningful caption for
each figure and cite sources near the claim they support. The [Markdown basics
reference](https://quarto.org/docs/authoring/markdown-basics.html) covers
tables, images, citations, cross-references, callouts, and other features.

## Why the Software Environment Matters

An analysis is a combination of source code and the software environment that
interprets it. Two computers can run the same source and obtain different
results when they use different Python versions, package versions, operating-
system libraries, or default settings. A result that cannot be rerun after an
environment changes is not fully reproducible, even when the code is available
[@wilson2017good].

An isolated environment makes these dependencies explicit and prevents one
project from silently changing another. Recording the Python version and the
installed packages lets a collaborator recreate the computational setting,
while a lockfile or pinned requirements file records the versions tested here.
This practice also makes failures diagnosable: when an upgrade changes an
output, we can identify the change instead of guessing which global installation
caused it.

## Python Environments for Quarto

Quarto executes Python through a Jupyter kernel, so the interpreter and
packages must be installed in an environment that Quarto can find. A virtual
environment keeps this project's packages separate from the system Python and
from unrelated projects.

This repository uses Python 3.12 as its tested compatibility target. The
recommended local environment is `.ids`, created and managed with `uv`. `uv`
is a fast command-line tool for installing Python versions, creating virtual
environments, and installing packages; it is not a replacement for Python or
Quarto. Students who prefer the standard Python tools can use the pip
alternative below.

```bash
uv venv --python 3.12 .ids
source .ids/bin/activate
uv pip install jupyter matplotlib pandas
```

The environment name is a convenience, not a requirement. Students may use a
different name, such as `.venv`, provided that Quarto and the editor use that
environment's Python kernel. When the name differs from the Makefile default,
pass the chosen name explicitly:

```bash
make req VENV=.venv
make render VENV=.venv
```

The first command records installed packages in `requirements.txt`; the second
renders the book. Do not install packages into the system Python, and do not
commit the virtual-environment directory. Keep the environment specification
and the source files under version control instead.

If `uv` is not available, create the environment with the standard library and
install the same packages with pip:

```bash
python3.12 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
python -m pip install --upgrade pip
python -m pip install jupyter matplotlib pandas
```

Use `python --version`, `which python`, and `jupyter kernelspec list` to verify
that the active interpreter is the one you intend to use. If Quarto reports
that it cannot find a kernel, select the environment's Python interpreter in
your editor or install its kernel with `python -m ipykernel install --user`.

## Reproducibility in Practice

Reproducibility requires a record of the inputs, environment, instructions, and
decisions that produced an analysis. A Quarto file brings prose and executable
code together, but it cannot by itself make an undocumented dataset,
unrecorded random seed, or unavailable package reproducible.

For each analysis, preserve these five components:

1. **Source:** the `.qmd` file and any scripts it calls.
2. **Data:** the source, version, download date, and transformations for each
   dataset; keep private or large raw data outside Git when necessary.
3. **Environment:** the Python version, package requirements, Quarto version,
   and operating-system details needed to run the source.
4. **Execution:** the commands, options, random seeds, and order of steps used
   to render the document.
5. **Outputs:** tables, figures, and conclusions checked against the source,
   not manually edited after rendering.

Use relative project paths, pin important package versions, set random seeds
when simulation is involved, and render from a clean working tree. These habits
make it possible for another analyst to inspect and repeat the work
[@wilson2017good].

## Rendering the Book

Rendering checks whether the source, computations, citations, and cross-
references work together. From the repository root, use the Makefile targets:

```bash
make check
make render
make preview
```

`make check` verifies the command-line tools, `make render` builds the complete
book in `_book/`, and `make preview` starts a local server with live reload.
For a quick test of one source file, use:

```bash
make render-one FILE=hello.qmd
```

Read the terminal output rather than assuming a successful command produced a
correct document. Check that code results make sense, links work, figures have
captions, citations resolve, and the output contains no accidental secrets or
local file paths. Generated `_book/`, `.quarto/`, and cache files belong in
`.gitignore`, not in a commit.

## Presentations with Quarto

Quarto presentations should replace the default habit of preparing course
work in a proprietary PowerPoint file. A presentation remains plain text,
versionable, reproducible, and reviewable while still producing a polished
slide deck. Quarto supports reveal.js slides in HTML and can also produce other
formats; the [presentation guide](https://quarto.org/docs/presentations/)
explains the available options.

A well-made Quarto homework is a reusable professional artifact, not a
disposable submission. The same source can become a polished report, research
memo, lab note, portfolio piece, or presentation for a different audience by
changing its format and explanation while retaining the executable analysis.
Students should therefore treat each assignment as an opportunity to practice
communicating evidence to people outside this course: clear prose, labeled
figures, citations, and a reproducible source record are more valuable than a
decorative layout alone [@quarto2025guide].

Excel, Word, and PowerPoint are useful office tools for administrative staff,
but they are not data-science authoring tools. Students should not author
data-science assignments in these MS Office formats: their binary contents
produce opaque diffs, make line-by-line review difficult, and can preserve
hidden formatting or manually edited results without recording how those
results were computed. Use a `.qmd` file, code, data description, and
environment as the authoritative record; an HTML rendering is the normal
output, and a PDF may be exported only when an audience or assignment
specifically requires it. The reason is methodological: a data-science
submission must expose executable transformations, preserve data and software
provenance, support line-by-line review, and reproduce the same outputs after
the source changes. Office files primarily preserve a presentation or a
spreadsheet state; they do not reliably preserve that computational record
[@wilson2017good].

Plain-text source and Git also provide benefits that office workflows lack.
Version history records who changed which lines and makes earlier versions
recoverable, rather than hiding revisions in a track-changes pane or a file
named `final-v2-revised`. Code automates repeated calculations, keeps tables
and figures synchronized with the data, and can be tested after each change.
Several people can review, merge, and reuse the same source without passing
around conflicting binary attachments.

Create a presentation by choosing a presentation format in the YAML header:

```markdown
---
title: "A Data-Science Result"
format: revealjs
---

## The question

What decision does this analysis support?

## The evidence

Explain the important figure and its limitations.
```

Render it with `quarto render presentation.qmd` or preview it with `quarto
preview presentation.qmd`. Use headings for slides, keep one central idea on
each slide, and write speaker notes when additional explanation belongs in the
oral presentation rather than on the slide. Export a PDF only when a course or
audience requires a static copy; keep the `.qmd` source as the authoritative
presentation.

## Exercises {.unnumbered}

Complete the Git setup from Chapter 2 and the Quarto installation from Chapter
1 before beginning. Document each exercise in a `.qmd` file as a user manual
for another beginner:

1. Build and inspect a reproducible Quarto document.
   a. Record your operating system, Python version, Quarto version, and any
      installation obstacle; explain how you verified that Quarto can find the
      Python environment.
   b. Create the environment, open the project in your editor, and reproduce the
      polar-axis line plot from the Quarto presentation guide with a caption.
   c. Add prose, an equation, an executable Python chunk, and a generated figure
      to a short document; render it to HTML, inspect it in a browser, and correct
      warnings or unresolved references.

2. Publish and preserve the work.
   a. Render the homework to PDF and place the PDF in a GitHub release, while
      keeping the `.qmd` source under version control and excluding the virtual
      environment and generated `_book/` output.
   b. Commit in small, meaningful steps and push the branch to your fork.
   c. Include the HTML link, release link, commands, and troubleshooting notes in
      the homework so another student can reproduce the result.
